titre: The Stomach Makes a Hormone That Announces a Meal Before It Starts
accroche: In 1999, Japanese researchers isolate an unknown peptide in rat stomach that triggers growth hormone: ghrelin.
contenu_vulgarise:
For a long time, appetite regulation seemed to rest on a single signal: leptin, discovered in 1994, which tells the brain that fat reserves are sufficient and that eating should stop. That signal explains the end of food intake, not its trigger, and an actor on the opposite side was missing.

## A peptide purified from rat stomach

In 1999, a Japanese team led by Masayasu Kojima looks for the natural ligand of the growth-hormone secretagogue receptor. Since the 1970s and 1980s, synthetic molecules had been known to trigger growth hormone release through this mechanism, without anyone knowing which substance activated it naturally in the body; the receptor itself had only been cloned three years earlier, in 1996. By purifying extracts from rat stomach, the team isolates a peptide of 28 amino acids carrying an unusual chemical modification on one of its amino acids, essential to its activity. Published in Nature, the result shows that this peptide, named ghrelin, does trigger growth hormone release, both in vivo and in vitro. The human version differs from the rat version by only two amino acids.

In 2001, an American team measures ghrelin in ten healthy volunteers at regular intervals over 24 hours. Its blood level nearly doubles just before each meal, then drops back within the following hour, a pattern exactly opposite to that of insulin.

## The missing counterpart to leptin

This second result shifts the significance of the 1999 discovery: ghrelin is not just a curiosity of growth-hormone biology, it is the hunger signal that appetite regulation had been missing since the discovery of leptin. The two hormones act in opposite directions on the same brain circuits, one announcing that it is time to eat, the other that it is time to stop.

The mechanism also shifts a common intuition, that of an empty stomach simply sending a mechanical signal of lack. Hunger is in fact anticipated: ghrelin rises before the stomach is empty, timed to the usual meal schedule rather than to its actual contents, which partly explains why hunger returns at a fixed time even when the last meal was a large one. This dual role, hunger signal and growth-hormone trigger, is also why some experimental obesity treatments aim to block the ghrelin receptor rather than the molecule itself, to blunt the sensation of hunger without depriving the body of growth hormone.

repere.texte: Ghrelin, isolated from rat stomach in 1999, is a 28-amino-acid peptide whose blood level nearly doubles before each meal in humans, before dropping back within the following hour.

carte.punch: Hunger has its own hormone too, and it climbs before the stomach is empty.
carte.idee: In 1999, a Japanese team isolates ghrelin from rat stomach, a peptide that stimulates growth hormone. In 2001, another team shows its level nearly doubles before each meal in humans: the missing counterpart to leptin, discovered in 1994.

quiz.question: Why did the 1999 discovery of ghrelin change the understanding of appetite regulation?
choix: Because it replaced leptin as the only known hormone in appetite regulation
Because it proves the stomach plays no role in the sensation of hunger
Because it revealed a hunger signal opposite to the satiety signal given by leptin
Because it showed that growth hormone depends on no specific receptor
quiz.explication: Leptin, discovered in 1994, signals satiety to the brain. Ghrelin, isolated in 1999, turned out to be the opposing hunger signal, its level nearly doubling before each meal in humans. The other three statements contradict the two studies cited in the entry.
